items.title: Standing hypotheses for ordinary character theory: $G$ finite, $k=\mathbb C$, and every representation finite-dimensional
The character $\chi_V(g)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_V(g))$ of a finite-dimensional complex representation
Class functions and the complex vector space $\mathrm{cf}(G)$
The standard inner product on $\mathrm{cf}(G)$
An irreducible complex character
The character table of a finite group
The tensor product of two complex representations
The dual or contragredient complex representation
The kernel of a complex character
For a complex character, $\chi(1)=\dim V$, $\chi$ is a class function, and $|\chi(g)|\le\chi(1)$ with equality exactly at scalars
items.strategy: Evaluate at the identity, use finite-order diagonalizability to write $\rho(g)$ with root-of-unity eigenvalues, apply the triangle inequality to their sum, and use trace invariance under similarity for conjugacy invariance.

items.title: The kernel of a complex character agrees with the kernel of any representation affording it
items.strategy: One implication is immediate. For the converse, the equality $\chi(g)=\chi(1)$ and the scalar-equality clause of the basic character proposition force $\rho(g)$ to be the identity.

items.title: Characters add on direct sums, multiply on tensor products, and conjugate on duals
items.strategy: Use block-diagonal trace additivity for direct sums, the trace-of-a-tensor-product identity for tensor products, and the inverse-transpose description of the dual action together with the basic character proposition for duals.

items.title: The character of a permutation representation counts fixed points
items.strategy: In the basis indexed by the underlying $G$-set, each group element acts by a permutation matrix, and the trace of that matrix is the number of diagonal ones, hence the number of fixed basis vectors.

items.title: The fixed subspace $V^G$ of a representation
The averaging operator projects onto the fixed subspace
items.strategy: Average the action operators over the finite group, check that left multiplication permutes the summands, and verify directly that the average fixes exactly the $G$-fixed vectors.

items.title: For finite-dimensional complex $V$, the intertwiners $V\to W$ are exactly the fixed points of $V^*\otimes W$
items.strategy: Use the published isomorphism $V^*\otimes W\cong\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)$ and compare the transported diagonal action with the standard conjugation action on linear maps, where fixed points are exactly the intertwiners.

items.title: The class-function inner product $\langle\chi_V,\chi_W\rangle$ equals $\dim\operatorname{Hom}_G(V,W)$
items.strategy: Identify $\operatorname{Hom}_G(V,W)$ with the fixed subspace of $V^*\otimes W$, apply the averaging projector, and compute its trace using the character formulas for duals and tensor products.

items.title: The first orthogonality relation for irreducible complex characters
items.strategy: Apply the intertwiner-dimension formula to irreducible representations and finish with Schur's lemma.

items.title: The irreducible complex characters form an orthonormal basis of $\mathrm{cf}(G)$
items.strategy: Row orthogonality gives an orthonormal family. The published RT-2 theorem gives the number of irreducibles, while class functions are determined by conjugacy classes, so the family has the full dimension of $\mathrm{cf}(G)$.

items.title: The multiplicity of an irreducible summand is a character inner product
items.strategy: Completely reduce the representation, expand its character as a sum of irreducible characters, and take inner products with the chosen irreducible character.

items.title: Finite-dimensional complex representations of a finite group are determined up to isomorphism by their characters
items.strategy: Completely reduce both representations and compare the multiplicity of every irreducible summand using the character-inner-product formula.

items.title: A complex character is irreducible if and only if its self-inner-product is $1$
items.strategy: Write the representation as a direct sum of irreducibles and sum the squares of the multiplicities furnished by the previous corollary.

items.title: The regular character is $|G|$ at $1$ and $0$ away from $1$
items.strategy: In the basis of group elements, the regular action is the permutation of $G$ by left translation, so the trace counts fixed points of that translation.

items.title: The regular character gives a second proof of the sum-of-squares formula
items.strategy: Take inner products of the regular character with each irreducible character to compute the multiplicities in the regular representation, then evaluate the resulting decomposition at the identity.

items.title: The second orthogonality relation for irreducible complex characters
items.strategy: Normalize the character-table columns by centralizer size so that the irreducible-character basis becomes a unitary matrix; column orthogonality is then the orthonormality of those normalized columns.

items.title: For $g\in G$, the sum of $|\chi_i(g)|^2$ over the irreducible complex characters is $|C_G(g)|$
items.strategy: Apply the second orthogonality relation with the same group element in both column slots.

items.title: The character table is square and invertible
items.strategy: The previous theorem gives mutually orthogonal normalized columns, so there are as many columns as rows and the character table matrix has inverse after the centralizer rescaling.

items.title: A representation with kernel containing a normal subgroup factors through the quotient, and irreducibility is unchanged by inflation
items.strategy: Define $\bar\rho(gN)=\rho(g)$, check well-definedness from $N\subseteq\ker\rho$, and note that the $\rho$-stable subspaces are exactly the $\bar\rho$-stable subspaces because the quotient map is surjective.

items.title: The normal subgroups of a finite group are exactly the intersections of kernels of irreducible complex characters
items.strategy: For a normal subgroup $N$, lift the irreducible representations of $G/N$ to $G$. Their common kernel is exactly $N$ because the regular representation of $G/N$ is faithful and completely reducible. The converse direction is immediate because character kernels are representation kernels.

items.title: A finite group is abelian if and only if all its irreducible complex characters have degree $1$
items.strategy: For abelian groups, use that $\mathbb C$ is a splitting field and every irreducible over a splitting field is one-dimensional. Conversely, combine the regular-character sum-of-squares formula with the published equality between the number of irreducibles and the number of conjugacy classes.

title: Characters and the Orthogonality Relations - Examples

items.title: The irreducible complex characters of a finite cyclic group are the $n$ powers of a primitive $n$th root
items.strategy: Identify irreducible characters of a cyclic group with homomorphisms to $\mathbb C^\times$, send a generator to an $n$th root of unity, and use the finite-abelian splitting-field theorem to see these are all of them.

items.title: The character table of a finite cyclic group over $\mathbb C$
items.strategy: Use the local description of the $n$ degree-one characters and Vieta's formula for $t^n-1$ to obtain the vanishing root sum, then write the table and check both orthogonality relations.

items.title: The standard representation of $S_n$ has character equal to the number of fixed points minus $1$
items.strategy: Subtract the trivial character from the permutation character of the action on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$.

items.title: $S_3$ has three irreducible complex characters of degrees $1$, $1$, and $2$
items.strategy: Use the three cycle-type classes of $S_3$, the trivial and sign characters, the standard character fixed-points-minus-one, and the sum-of-squares formula to see no other irreducible degrees occur.

items.title: The character table of $S_3$
items.strategy: Use the local degree data and the three cycle-type classes to write the table, then verify both orthogonality relations directly.

items.title: The square of the two-dimensional $S_3$ character decomposes as $1+\operatorname{sgn}+\chi_2$
items.strategy: Square the two-dimensional row by the tensor-product character formula and recover the irreducible multiplicities by inner products with the $S_3$ table.

items.title: $A_4$ has a normal Klein four subgroup and four conjugacy classes
items.strategy: Write the Klein four subgroup of double transpositions, use the quotient of order three, and apply the alternating-group class-splitting criterion to separate the two classes of $3$-cycles.

items.title: The character table of $A_4$
items.strategy: Use the normal Klein four subgroup to obtain the three lifted degree-one characters from the quotient of order three, then recover the remaining degree-three row from orthogonality and the sum-of-squares formula.

items.title: $S_4$ has five conjugacy classes of sizes $1$, $6$, $3$, $8$, and $6$
items.strategy: Use the cycle-type classification in $S_4$ and the symmetric-group class equation to read off the five conjugacy classes and their sizes.

items.title: The character table of $S_4$ and the normal subgroups it reveals
items.strategy: Use the conjugacy-class data, the permutation character on four letters, its sign twist, and orthogonality to complete the table; then intersect character kernels to recover the normal subgroups.

items.title: The character table of $Q_8$
items.strategy: Use the unique involution and the abelianization $Q_8/Z(Q_8)\cong C_2\times C_2$ to obtain the four degree-one rows, then determine the remaining degree-two row from orthogonality and the sum-of-squares formula.

items.title: The character table of $\operatorname{Dih}(C_4)$
items.strategy: Use the dihedral presentation and abelianization to obtain the four degree-one rows, then determine the remaining degree-two row from orthogonality and the sum-of-squares formula.

items.title: FALSE: nonisomorphic finite groups always have different character tables
items.strategy: Refute the claim by placing the $Q_8$ and $\operatorname{Dih}(C_4)$ tables side by side: the tables agree even though the groups are distinguished by their involution structure.

items.title: FALSE: a complex character of a finite group is always a group homomorphism
items.strategy: Use the two-dimensional irreducible character of $S_3$: its value $0$ on a transposition cannot lie in a multiplicative image of a homomorphism to $\mathbb C^\times$.

items.title: FALSE: every value of an irreducible complex character is real
items.strategy: The nontrivial one-dimensional rows of the $A_4$ table take the primitive cube roots of unity on the 3-cycles.

items.title: FALSE: distinct irreducible complex characters of a finite group have distinct degrees
items.strategy: The $Q_8$ table already contains four distinct irreducible characters of degree $1$.

items.title: FALSE: every complex class function with self-inner-product $1$ is a character
items.strategy: If $\chi$ is a character, then $-\chi$ has the same self-inner-product but is not a character because its value at the identity is negative.
